claim: NAD+ is a cofactor for sirtuins and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs), enzymes which regulate numerous important cellular functions.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published works (Cantó et al., 2015; Verdin, 2015; Peek et al., 2013).

claim: NAD(P) is compartmentalized and present as free and protein-bound fractions within cells.
source: NAD(P) is compartmentalized and present as free and protein-bound fractions within cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The majority of pyridine nucleotides is known to be protein-bound.
source: However, the results obtained by these methods have limited physiological relevance because the majority of pyridine nucleotides is known to be protein-bound (Zhang et al., 2002) and have different distribution between cytosol and mitochondria (Williamson et al., 1967).

claim: Pyridine nucleotides have different distribution between cytosol and mitochondria.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Williamson et al., 1967.

claim: SoNar and iNAP are bright, ratiometric and show a large dynamic range.
source: SoNar and iNAP, two fluorescent sensors for measuring free NAD+/NADH and NADPH, respectively, are particularly well performing NAD(P) sensors as they are bright, ratiometric and show a large dynamic range.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of existing sensors based on established knowledge.

claim: SoNar and iNAP are based on inserting cpYFP into the redox-sensing transcriptional repressor Rex.
source: SoNar and iNAP are based on inserting cpYFP into the redox-sensing transcriptional repressor Rex (Zhao et al., 2015; Tao et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhao et al., 2015 and Tao et al., 2017.

claim: SoNar and iNAP require excitation at short wavelengths (420 nm and 480 nm).
source: However, both sensors require excitation at short wavelengths (420 nm and 480 nm) and the fluorescence signal upon excitation at 480 nm is pH-dependent.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing sensors based on established knowledge.

claim: The fluorescence signal of SoNar and iNAP upon excitation at 480 nm is pH-dependent.
source: However, both sensors require excitation at short wavelengths (420 nm and 480 nm) and the fluorescence signal upon excitation at 480 nm is pH-dependent.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing sensors based on established knowledge.

claim: A sensor for measuring free NAD+ has been generated by fusing a bipartite NAD+-binding protein to cpVenus.
source: A sensor for measuring free NAD+ has been generated by fusing a bipartite NAD+-binding protein to cpVenus (Cambronne et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cambronne et al., 2016.

claim: The cpVenus-based NAD+ sensor shows a modest two-fold dynamic range.
source: While being the first sensor able to measure free, compartmentalized NAD+, it only shows a modest two-fold dynamic range and requires excitation at 405 and 488 nm.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of an existing sensor based on established knowledge.

claim: The cpVenus-based NAD+ sensor requires excitation at 405 and 488 nm.
source: While being the first sensor able to measure free, compartmentalized NAD+, it only shows a modest two-fold dynamic range and requires excitation at 405 and 488 nm.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of an existing sensor based on established knowledge.

claim: The pH sensitivity of the fluorescence signal of the cpVenus-based NAD+ sensor between pH 7.4 to 8 is comparable to its dynamic range.
source: Furthermore, the pH sensitivity of the fluorescence signal of the sensor between pH 7.4 to 8 is comparable to its dynamic range.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of an existing sensor based on established knowledge.

claim: No sensors exist to measure free NADPH/NADP+.
source: In addition, none of the sensors introduced so far permits a rational adaption of their response range and no sensors exist to measure free NADPH/NADP+.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in existing sensor technology based on knowledge of the field.

claim: The new semisynthetic biosensors are ratiometric.
source: The sensors are ratiometric, display large dynamic ranges, are pH-insensitive, possess tunable response range and can be excited at long wavelengths (560 nm).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the properties of the sensors developed in this work.

claim: The new semisynthetic biosensors display large dynamic ranges.
source: The sensors are ratiometric, display large dynamic ranges, are pH-insensitive, possess tunable response range and can be excited at long wavelengths (560 nm).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the properties of the sensors developed in this work.

claim: The new semisynthetic biosensors are pH-insensitive.
source: The sensors are ratiometric, display large dynamic ranges, are pH-insensitive, possess tunable response range and can be excited at long wavelengths (560 nm).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the properties of the sensors developed in this work.

claim: The new semisynthetic biosensors possess tunable response range.
source: The sensors are ratiometric, display large dynamic ranges, are pH-insensitive, possess tunable response range and can be excited at long wavelengths (560 nm).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the properties of the sensors developed in this work.

claim: The new semisynthetic biosensors can be excited at long wavelengths (560 nm).
source: The sensors are ratiometric, display large dynamic ranges, are pH-insensitive, possess tunable response range and can be excited at long wavelengths (560 nm).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the properties of the sensors developed in this work.

claim: Snifits contain an analyte-binding protein and two self-labeling protein tags.
source: Snifits contain an analyte-binding protein and two self-labeling protein tags, for example SNAP-tag (Keppler et al., 2003) and Halo-tag (Los et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the design principle of Snifits, with citations to the original SNAP-tag and Halo-tag publications.

claim: Human sepiapterin reductase (SPR) was selected as NADP-binding protein for the design of NAD(P)-Snifits.
source: For the design of NAD(P)-Snifits, we selected human sepiapterin reductase (SPR) as NADP-binding protein.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the design choice made in this work.

claim: Sulfa drugs such as sulfapyridine and sulfamethoxazole form a ternary complex with SPR in the presence of NADP+, but not with NADPH.
source: These potent SPR inhibitors such as sulfapyridine and sulfamethoxazole form a ternary complex with the enzyme in the presence of NADP+, but not with NADPH (Figure 1a) (Chidley et al., 2011; Haruki et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chidley et al., 2011 and Haruki et al., 2012, and referenced in Figure 1a.

claim: The π-stacking interaction between the sulfa drug and the nicotinamide moiety of NADP+ can be exploited to generate a semisynthetic biosensor for NADP+.
source: We speculated that the π-stacking interaction between the sulfa drug and the nicotinamide moiety of NADP+ could be exploited to generate a semisynthetic biosensor for NADP+ (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: This is a design hypothesis that was tested in this work, referenced in Figures 1a and 1b.

claim: The pyridine moiety of sulfapyridine and the nicotinamide moiety of NADP+ are at a suitable distance (3.3 Å) for efficient π-stacking.
source: The pyridine moiety of sulfapyridine (SPY) and the nicotinamide moiety of NADP+ are at a suitable distance (3.3 Å) for efficient π-stacking.
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption for Figure 1a, which shows structural data from PDB entry 4HWK.

claim: Labeling of the fusion protein SPR-Halo-p30-SNAP with CP-TMR-SMX has a second-order rate constant of 3.9∙10^4 M^−1s^−1.
source: Labeling of the fusion protein SPR-Halo-p30-SNAP with CP-TMR-SMX and SiR-Halo was fast, with second-order rate constants of 3.9∙104 and 2.5∙105 M−1s−1, respectively (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is experimental data reported in the manuscript and referenced in Appendix 1—table 1.

claim: Labeling of the fusion protein SPR-Halo-p30-SNAP with SiR-Halo has a second-order rate constant of 2.5∙10^5 M^−1s^−1.
source: Labeling of the fusion protein SPR-Halo-p30-SNAP with CP-TMR-SMX and SiR-Halo was fast, with second-order rate constants of 3.9∙104 and 2.5∙105 M−1s−1, respectively (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is experimental data reported in the manuscript and referenced in Appendix 1—table 1.

claim: NADP-Snifit shows a maximum 8.9 ± 0.1 fold FRET ratio change upon titration with NADP+.
source: Titration of the resulting NADP-Snifit with NADP+ revealed a maximum 8.9 ± 0.1 fold FRET ratio change (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figures 2a and 2b.

claim: The concentration resulting in the half-maximal sensor response (c50) of NADP-Snifit was determined to be 29 ± 7 nM.
source: The concentration resulting in the half-maximal sensor response (c50) was determined to be 29 ± 7 nM (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figures 2a and 2b.

claim: No binding of intramolecular ligand was detectable in the absence of NADP+.
source: No binding of intramolecular ligand was detectable in the absence of NADP+ (Appendix 1—Figure 1a).
evidence: This is experimental data referenced in Appendix 1—Figure 1a.

claim: The intramolecular ligand does not bind to the binary complex of SPR:NADPH.
source: Titration of the sensor with NADPH showed that the intramolecular ligand does not bind to the binary complex of SPR:NADPH, presumably due to the absence of the π-stacking interaction (Appendix 1—Figure 1b).
evidence: This is experimental data referenced in Appendix 1—Figure 1b, with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: The half-maximal sensor response (r50) of NADP-Snifit corresponds to a NADPH/NADP+ ratio of 30 ± 3.
source: Titration of the sensor with varying NADPH/NADP+ ratios showed that the half-maximal sensor response (r50) corresponds to a ratio of 30 ± 3 (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Cellular free NADPH/NADP+ values have been reported to be between 10 and 100.
source: As cellular free NADPH/NADP+ values have been reported to be between 10 and 100 (Veech et al., 1969; Hedeskov et al., 1987; Zhang et al., 2015), NADP-Snifit in cells would report on free NADPH/NADP+ and not free NADP+.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Veech et al., 1969; Hedeskov et al., 1987; Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: NADP-Snifit in cells would report on free NADPH/NADP+ and not free NADP+.
source: As cellular free NADPH/NADP+ values have been reported to be between 10 and 100 (Veech et al., 1969; Hedeskov et al., 1987; Zhang et al., 2015), NADP-Snifit in cells would report on free NADPH/NADP+ and not free NADP+.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sensor's r50 value and known cellular NADPH/NADP+ ratios.

claim: SPR belongs to the short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) superfamily.
source: SPR belongs to the short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) superfamily and has a characteristic Rossmann fold as dinucleotide-binding domain (Kallberg et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kallberg et al., 2010.

claim: SPR has a characteristic Rossmann fold as dinucleotide-binding domain.
source: SPR belongs to the short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) superfamily and has a characteristic Rossmann fold as dinucleotide-binding domain (Kallberg et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kallberg et al., 2010.

claim: Enzymes specific for NADP generally possess two conserved arginines or lysines interacting with the 2'-phosphate group and the adenine moiety.
source: Enzymes specific for NADP, such as SPR, generally possess two conserved arginines or lysines interacting with the 2'-phosphate group and the adenine moiety.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about enzyme specificity.

claim: Enzymes specific for NAD have a conserved aspartate that interacts with 2'- and 3'-hydroxyl groups in a bidentate manner.
source: Enzymes specific for NAD, such as 15-hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase (PGDH), have a conserved aspartate that interacts with 2'- and 3'-hydroxyl groups in a bidentate manner (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about enzyme specificity, illustrated in Figure 1d.

claim: The mutations A41D and R42W were introduced into SPR to switch the cofactor specificity of NADP-Snifit.
source: Guided by sequence and structure comparison of SPR and PGDH (Tanaka et al., 1996), we switched the cofactor specificity of NADP-Snift by introducing the mutations A41D and R42W into SPR.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design, with a citation to Tanaka et al., 1996.

claim: NAD-Snifit is specific for NAD+ with a c50 of 63 ± 12 µM.
source: Titrations of the resulting NAD-Snifit with either NAD+ or NADP+ showed that the sensor was specific for NAD+ with a c50 of 63 ± 12 µM while conserving the 8-fold maximum ratio change of NADP-Snifit (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: NAD-Snifit conserves the 8-fold maximum ratio change of NADP-Snifit.
source: Titrations of the resulting NAD-Snifit with either NAD+ or NADP+ showed that the sensor was specific for NAD+ with a c50 of 63 ± 12 µM while conserving the 8-fold maximum ratio change of NADP-Snifit (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: NAD-Snifit did not show any response to NADP+ up to concentrations of 1 mM.
source: NAD-Snifit did not show any response to NADP+ up to concentrations of 1 mM.
evidence: This is experimental data demonstrating the specificity of NAD-Snifit.

claim: The reported free cytosolic NAD+ of mammalian cells is around 100 µM.
source: Under physiological conditions, the reported free cytosolic NAD+ of mammalian cells is around 100 µM (Zhang et al., 2002; Cambronne et al., 2016) and the NAD+/NADH ratio has been reported to be 100–600 (Veech et al., 1969; Zhao et al., 2015) in the cytosol and 4–10 (Veech et al., 1969; Williamson et al., 1967) in the mitochondria.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2002 and Cambronne et al., 2016.

claim: The NAD+/NADH ratio has been reported to be 100–600 in the cytosol.
source: Under physiological conditions, the reported free cytosolic NAD+ of mammalian cells is around 100 µM (Zhang et al., 2002; Cambronne et al., 2016) and the NAD+/NADH ratio has been reported to be 100–600 (Veech et al., 1969; Zhao et al., 2015) in the cytosol and 4–10 (Veech et al., 1969; Williamson et al., 1967) in the mitochondria.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Veech et al., 1969 and Zhao et al., 2015.

claim: The NAD+/NADH ratio has been reported to be 4–10 in the mitochondria.
source: Under physiological conditions, the reported free cytosolic NAD+ of mammalian cells is around 100 µM (Zhang et al., 2002; Cambronne et al., 2016) and the NAD+/NADH ratio has been reported to be 100–600 (Veech et al., 1969; Zhao et al., 2015) in the cytosol and 4–10 (Veech et al., 1969; Williamson et al., 1967) in the mitochondria.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Veech et al., 1969 and Williamson et al., 1967.

claim: NAD-Snifit in cells would report on free NAD+ levels.
source: In cells, NAD-Snifit would thus report on free NAD+ levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sensor's c50 value and known cellular NAD+ concentrations.

claim: Both NADP-Snifit and NAD-Snifit show negligible pH sensitivity between pH 6.8 and 8.
source: In addition, both sensors show negligible pH sensitivity between pH 6.8 and 8 (Figure 2b and Appendix 1—Figure 1c).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2b and Appendix 1—Figure 1c.

claim: Both sensors displayed a two-fold increase of their c50 values when raising the temperature from 25°C to 37°C.
source: While both sensors displayed a two-fold increase of their c50 values when raising the temperature from 25°C to 37°C (Appendix 1—Figure 1e, f), the r50 of NADP-Snifit was not affected by such temperature changes (Appendix 1—Figure 1g), indicating that the affinities of SPR for NADPH and NADP+ display similar temperature dependencies.
evidence: This is experimental data referenced in Appendix 1—Figure 1e, f.

claim: The r50 of NADP-Snifit was not affected by temperature changes from 25°C to 37°C.
source: While both sensors displayed a two-fold increase of their c50 values when raising the temperature from 25°C to 37°C (Appendix 1—Figure 1e, f), the r50 of NADP-Snifit was not affected by such temperature changes (Appendix 1—Figure 1g), indicating that the affinities of SPR for NADPH and NADP+ display similar temperature dependencies.
evidence: This is experimental data referenced in Appendix 1—Figure 1g.

claim: The affinities of SPR for NADPH and NADP+ display similar temperature dependencies.
source: While both sensors displayed a two-fold increase of their c50 values when raising the temperature from 25°C to 37°C (Appendix 1—Figure 1e, f), the r50 of NADP-Snifit was not affected by such temperature changes (Appendix 1—Figure 1g), indicating that the affinities of SPR for NADPH and NADP+ display similar temperature dependencies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that r50 is not affected by temperature changes.

claim: The opening of closed NADP-Snifit bound with NADP+ follows first-order kinetics with a half-life t1/2 of 25 ± 1 s.
source: The opening of closed NADP-Snifit bound with NADP+ follows first-order kinetics with a half-life t1/2 of 25 ± 1 s, whereas the closing of open sensor upon binding of NADP+ is much faster with a t1/2 of <1 s (Appendix 1—Figure 1h, i).
evidence: This is experimental data referenced in Appendix 1—Figure 1h, i.

claim: The closing of open NADP-Snifit upon binding of NADP+ has a t1/2 of <1 s.
source: The opening of closed NADP-Snifit bound with NADP+ follows first-order kinetics with a half-life t1/2 of 25 ± 1 s, whereas the closing of open sensor upon binding of NADP+ is much faster with a t1/2 of <1 s (Appendix 1—Figure 1h, i).
evidence: This is experimental data referenced in Appendix 1—Figure 1h, i.

claim: The kinetics of NAD-Snifit should be at least as fast as those of NADP-Snifit.
source: As NAD-Snifit has a 1000-fold lower affinity for its cofactor than NADP-Snifit, we assume that the kinetics of NAD-Snifit should be at least as fast as those of NADP-Snifit.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lower affinity of NAD-Snifit for its cofactor.

claim: Both NADP-Snifit and NAD-Snifit are suitable to monitor fluctuations of NADPH/NADP+ and NAD+ on the time scale of seconds.
source: Accordingly, both NADP-Snifit and NAD-Snifit are suitable to monitor fluctuations of NADPH/NADP+ and NAD+ on the time scale of seconds.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured kinetics of the sensors.

claim: Replacing the tethered sulfamethoxazole with sulfachloropyridazine raised the c50 of NADP-Snifit from 29 ± 7 nM to 1.9 ± 0.3 µM.
source: Replacing the tethered sulfamethoxazole with sulfachloropyridazine, a ligand with lower affinity to SPR, raised the c50 of NADP-Snifit from 29 ± 7 nM to 1.9 ± 0.3 µM (Appendix 1—figure 1j, k).
evidence: This is experimental data referenced in Appendix 1—figure 1j, k.

claim: Intracellular labeling efficiency of SiR-Halo was 100%.
source: The labeling efficiency of SiR-Halo was 100% and of CP-TMR-SMX 92% (Appendix 1—figure 3a, b).
evidence: This is experimental data referenced in Appendix 1—figure 3a, b.

claim: Intracellular labeling efficiency of CP-TMR-SMX was 92%.
source: The labeling efficiency of SiR-Halo was 100% and of CP-TMR-SMX 92% (Appendix 1—figure 3a, b).
evidence: This is experimental data referenced in Appendix 1—figure 3a, b.

claim: Calibration curves of FRET ratio versus NADP+ of NADP-Snifits, labeled in vitro either with 20% or 100% of CP-TMR-SMX, fully overlay.
source: Calibration curves of FRET ratio versus NADP+ of NADP-Snifits, labeled in vitro either with 20% or 100% of CP-TMR-SMX, fully overlay (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The FRET ratio was shown to be largely independent of the intensity of the TMR or SiR signals in flow cytometry experiments.
source: In such experiments, the FRET ratio was shown to be largely independent of the intensity of the TMR or SiR signals, indicating that neither variations in labeling efficiency nor expression level affect quantitative analysis.
evidence: This is an observation from flow cytometry experiments.

claim: The intracellular sensor concentration reached in different cellular compartments is in the low micromolar range (1–5 µM).
source: We determined the intracellular sensor concentration reached in different cellular compartments to be in the low micromolar range (1–5 µM) (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is experimental data referenced in Appendix 1—table 2.

claim: Several dehydrogenases are among the most abundant cellular proteins.
source: Several dehydrogenases are among the most abundant cellular proteins (Beck et al., 2011), and there is a large pool of proteins that buffer NAD(P) (Zhang et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Beck et al., 2011 and Zhang et al., 2002.

claim: There is a large pool of proteins that buffer NAD(P).
source: Several dehydrogenases are among the most abundant cellular proteins (Beck et al., 2011), and there is a large pool of proteins that buffer NAD(P) (Zhang et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2002.

claim: SPR itself is a highly abundant protein in U2OS cells.
source: In U2OS cells, SPR itself is a highly abundant protein (Beck et al., 2011), and we determined comparable high levels of endogenous SPR in a number of different cell lines (Appendix 1—figure 3c, d).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Beck et al., 2011 and experimental data in Appendix 1—figure 3c, d.

claim: Comparable high levels of endogenous SPR were determined in a number of different cell lines.
source: In U2OS cells, SPR itself is a highly abundant protein (Beck et al., 2011), and we determined comparable high levels of endogenous SPR in a number of different cell lines (Appendix 1—figure 3c, d).
evidence: This is experimental data referenced in Appendix 1—figure 3c, d.

claim: The additional buffering produced by the presence of the sensor protein in the low micromolar range should be negligible.
source: Thus, the additional buffering produced by the presence of the sensor protein in the low micromolar range should be negligible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high abundance of endogenous NAD(P)-binding proteins.

claim: Free intracellular NAD+ in U2OS cells was found to be around 70–120 µM.
source: With respect to free NAD+ levels, free intracellular NAD+ in U2OS cells was found to be around 70–120 µM.
evidence: This is experimental data from the quantification experiments.

claim: Free cytosolic NAD+ of the different cell lines were found to be relatively similar, ranging from 40 to 70 µM.
source: Free cytosolic NAD+ of the different cell lines were found to be relatively similar, ranging from 40 to 70 µM (Table 1, Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Table 1 and Appendix 1—table 3.

claim: The free NAD+ values obtained in this study are in agreement with previously reported values for HEK293 cells, obtained with the cpVenus-based NAD+ sensor.
source: These results are in agreement with previously reported values for HEK293 cells, obtained with the cpVenus-based NAD+ sensor (Cambronne et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison with published data, supported by a citation to Cambronne et al., 2016.

claim: Free NADPH/NADP+ is maintained at a high ratio inside cells.
source: With respect to NADPH/NADP+, we discovered that free NADPH/NADP+ is maintained at a high ratio inside cells while the reduction potential of mitochondria is significantly higher than that of the cytosol and the nucleus (Table 1).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The reduction potential of mitochondria is significantly higher than that of the cytosol and the nucleus.
source: With respect to NADPH/NADP+, we discovered that free NADPH/NADP+ is maintained at a high ratio inside cells while the reduction potential of mitochondria is significantly higher than that of the cytosol and the nucleus (Table 1).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Free cytosolic NADPH/NADP+ ratios in the different cell lines varied up to 4-fold, ranging from 20 to 80.
source: Free cytosolic NADPH/NADP+ ratios in the different cell lines varied up to 4-fold, ranging from 20 to 80 (Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This is experimental data referenced in Appendix 1—table 3.

claim: This is the first time that free, cellular NADPH/NADP+ is directly quantified.
source: To our knowledge, it is the first time that free, cellular NADPH/NADP+ is directly quantified and that a difference in this ratio between cytosol and mitochondria is demonstrated.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: This is the first time that a difference in NADPH/NADP+ ratio between cytosol and mitochondria is demonstrated.
source: To our knowledge, it is the first time that free, cellular NADPH/NADP+ is directly quantified and that a difference in this ratio between cytosol and mitochondria is demonstrated.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The higher ratio of NADPH/NADP+ in mitochondria could be due to the higher pH in that organelle, pushing mitochondrial NAD(P) transhydrogenase and dehydrogenases towards the formation of NADPH.
source: The higher ratio of NADPH/NADP+ in mitochondria could, at least partially, be due to the higher pH in that organelle, pushing mitochondrial NAD(P) transhydrogenase and dehydrogenases towards the formation of NADPH (Rydström, 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation to Rydström, 2006.

claim: H2O2 is a reactive oxygen species (ROS) that is metabolized into H2O and O2 by different enzymes of the antioxidant system such as catalase, glutathione peroxidase and peroxiredoxin.
source: H2O2 is a reactive oxygen species (ROS) that is metabolized into H2O and O2 by different enzymes of the antioxidant system such as catalase, glutathione peroxidase and peroxiredoxin (Veal et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Veal et al., 2007.

claim: The resulting oxidized glutathione and thioredoxin are recycled by NADPH-dependent glutathione and thioredoxin reductase.
source: The resulting oxidized glutathione and thioredoxin are recycled by NADPH-dependent glutathione and thioredoxin reductase, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cellular antioxidant systems.

claim: Fluctuations in H2O2 can directly influence NADPH/NADP+.
source: Therefore, fluctuations in H2O2 can directly influence NADPH/NADP+.
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of NADPH in recycling oxidized glutathione and thioredoxin.

claim: Perfusion of H2O2 produces a rapid decrease of the FRET ratio, corresponding to a decrease in NADPH/NADP+.
source: Perfusion of H2O2 produces a rapid decrease of the FRET ratio, corresponding to a decrease in NADPH/NADP+ (Figure 3).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: H2O2 itself does not influence the sensor response.
source: H2O2 itself does not influence the sensor response (Appendix 1—figure 1p).
evidence: This is experimental data referenced in Appendix 1—figure 1p.

claim: At the start of the experiment, free cytosolic NADPH/NADP+ ratio was around 70.
source: At the start of the experiment, free cytosolic NADPH/NADP+ ratio was around 70 and incubation with 10 µM H2O2 lowers the NADPH/NADP+ ratio to about 35 (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Incubation with 10 µM H2O2 lowers the NADPH/NADP+ ratio to about 35.
source: At the start of the experiment, free cytosolic NADPH/NADP+ ratio was around 70 and incubation with 10 µM H2O2 lowers the NADPH/NADP+ ratio to about 35 (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Incubation with 100 or 200 µM H2O2 decreased the NADPH/NADP+ ratio down to 20.
source: Incubation with even higher concentrations of H2O2 (100 or 200 µM H2O2) decreased the ratio further down to 20.
evidence: This is experimental data from the H2O2 perfusion experiments.

claim: The decrease of NADPH/NADP+ reached a plateau within 5 min.
source: The decrease of NADPH/NADP+ reached a plateau within 5 min.
evidence: This is experimental data from the H2O2 perfusion experiments.

claim: H2O2 scavenging by glutathione-thioredoxin antioxidant systems is a rapid and efficient process that occurs faster than regeneration of NADPH.
source: The amplitude and kinetic of the NADPH/NADP+ changes indicate that H2O2 scavenging by glutathione-thioredoxin antioxidant systems is a rapid and efficient process that occurs faster than regeneration of NADPH.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed kinetics of NADPH/NADP+ changes.

claim: Cells even after incubation with 200 µM H2O2 maintain a cytosolic free NADPH/NADP+ ratio of >10.
source: The observation that cells even after incubation with 200 µM H2O2 maintain a cytosolic free NADPH/NADP+ ratio of >10 indicates a remarkable capacity of cells to regenerate NADPH.
evidence: This is experimental data from the H2O2 perfusion experiments.

claim: Cells have a remarkable capacity to regenerate NADPH.
source: The observation that cells even after incubation with 200 µM H2O2 maintain a cytosolic free NADPH/NADP+ ratio of >10 indicates a remarkable capacity of cells to regenerate NADPH.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cells maintain high NADPH/NADP+ ratios even under oxidative stress.

claim: A decrease in NADPH/NADP+ ratio activates glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase.
source: A decrease in NADPH/NADP+ ratio activates glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (Patra and Hay, 2014) resulting in a dynamic rerouting of metabolic flux from glycolysis to the pentose phosphate pathway (Ralser et al., 2007; Kuehne et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Patra and Hay, 2014; Ralser et al., 2007; Kuehne et al., 2015.

claim: A decrease in NADPH/NADP+ ratio results in a dynamic rerouting of metabolic flux from glycolysis to the pentose phosphate pathway.
source: A decrease in NADPH/NADP+ ratio activates glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (Patra and Hay, 2014) resulting in a dynamic rerouting of metabolic flux from glycolysis to the pentose phosphate pathway (Ralser et al., 2007; Kuehne et al., 2015).
